paper_title: EAU: Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution for Training User-Centric Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Training LLM agents to interact with users over multiple turns is challenging because the learning signal depends not only on the agent, but also on the user simulator and environment, which jointly shape the agent's experience. Simulated users can be stochastic or inconsistent, while environments may contain unreliable tools, incomplete state coverage, and incorrect verifiers. Prior work mainly addresses the resulting instability through reward shaping or denser supervision, while treating these components as fixed. We instead introduce EAU, a meta-agent framework for environment--agent--user co-evolution. During training, EAU monitors trajectories, tool traces, rewards, and training statistics; diagnoses failures and uninformative interactions; and proposes targeted modifications to the user simulator, environment, reward design, and RL configuration. Validated changes are hot-swapped into the ongoing run, allowing the training setup to evolve together with the policy. These adaptations also persist across runs, so later training can build on previously discovered improvements rather than restarting from a fixed setup. We enable this process through an editable symbolic representation of user and environment dynamics, while the agent remains a neural LLM optimized with RL. Across three interactive-agent benchmarks and two backbone models, EAU consistently outperforms prior RL methods, improving the overall score over the strongest baseline by 14.7--15.0% and increasing successful task completion on ColBench by up to 36.7%, showing that co-evolving the training system with the policy can substantially improve multi-turn RL.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language models are increasingly deployed as agents that collaborate with humans rather than simply execute fully specified tasks. As shown in Figure 2, in many realistic applications, users can provide incomplete or evolving specifications, requiring an agent to interact over multiple turns: asking clarifying questions, resolving ambiguities, negotiating constraints, and adapting its behavior as new information emerges. This has motivated growing body of interactive benchmarks in which agents communicate with simulated users while acting in an external environment (Yao et al., 2024; Barres et al., 2025; Qian et al., 2025a). Such simulation makes large-scale evaluation and reinforcement learning (RL) possible, but it also introduces fundamental challenge: the learning signal is only as reliable as the interaction that produces it. LLM-based user simulators are stochastic and can behave inconsistently, for example by drifting from their assigned persona, revealing information prematurely, or changing their intent across otherwise similar episodes. At the same time, environments may contain incomplete state coverage, unreliable tool behavior, unreachable tasks, or incorrect verifiers. Moreover, because both components are typically fixed throughout training, the interactions they generate need not remain informative as the policy evolves. Together, these issues can make rewards highly variable or systematically misleading, substantially destabilizing RL for interactive agents. Prior work has largely addressed this instability by improving the supervision presented to the policy, for example through reward shaping that credits partial progress (Qian et al., 2025b) or auxiliary supervision that provides denser learning signals (Kong et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). These approaches can make better use of noisy signal, but they leave the sources of that signalthe user simulator and the environment largely unchanged. We argue that this misses an important root cause of instability. If tool silently fails for particular argument, verifier incorrectly rejects successful trajectory, or simulated user reveals information that the agent was supposed to elicit, modifying the downstream reward cannot recover the intended interaction. More generally, as the policy improves, fixed simulator and environment may continue producing trajectories that are redundant, uninformative, or poorly targeted to the policys current weaknesses. We therefore propose shifting part of the intervention upstream: rather than treating the user simulator and environment as fixed infrastructure and optimizing only the policys learning signal, we continually diagnose and revise the interaction process itself during training. Figure 2: Illustration of usercentric agentic task. An agent needs to ask for clarifications about user query. To realize this idea, we introduce EAU, meta-agent that continuously supervises RL training and improves the components that generate its learning experience. Throughout training, EAU observes rollout transcripts, tool traces, rewards, and aggregate training statistics, and diagnoses whether problematic or uninformative trajectories arise from the policy, the user simulator, the environment, or the training configuration. As shown in Figure 1, it proposes targeted interventions based on this diagnosis, including correcting environment or verifier failures, refining the simulators persona and information-disclosure behavior, and adjusting reward terms or training hyperparameters. Importantly, these interventions are not limited to fixing errors. As the policy improves, EAU can also adapt the simulator and environment to expose unresolved weaknesses and generate more informative training trajectories. Candidate modifications are validated by bounded integrity gate before being accepted and hot-swapped into the ongoing training loop, allowing the training system itself to evolve without repeatedly restarting from scratch. This produces different view of interactive-agent training: rather than optimizing policy against fixed user and environment, EAU enables the training system to adapt alongside policy learning. Instead of prescribing fixed sequence of component updates, the meta-agent diagnoses emerging problems and determines what to modify and when to intervene. Simulator revisions, reward and curriculum adjustments, hyperparameter changes, and implementation repairs are therefore part of Preprint: EAU, Meta-Agent for Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution the intervention space. The contribution lies in enabling and organizing this adaptive process during and across training runs. We evaluate EAU on three interactive-agent benchmarks and two backbone models. Across these settings, EAU discovers interpretable modifications to both simulators and environments and improves final agent performance by up to 36.7% over the previous state of the art, while our analysis shows how the three components evolve together throughout training. To summarize, our contributions are: We identify fixed user simulators and environments as key bottleneck in interactive RL. We introduce EAU, meta-agent that diagnoses and updates the training system online. We demonstrate improved agent performance on three user-centric benchmarks, with targeted analyses of symbolic-user mixing, intra-run intervention, and alternative training algorithms and meta-agent implementations.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: User Centric Agentic Reinforcement Learning. User-centric tasks (Yao et al., 2024; Barres et al., 2025; Qian et al., 2025a) focus on interacting and fulfilling the requirement of simulated user under multi-turn conversations. Different from previous multi-turn Reinforcement Learning (Jimenez et al., 2024; Xi et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b) that solely interacts with fixed deterministic environment, user-centric RL (Qian et al., 2025b; Kong et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026) poses an additional challenge: the introduction of LLM user simulator may cause several issues such as stochastic state transition, inconsistent behaviors and collapse in training due to overfitting fixed behavior (Yu et al., 2026). Recent methods mainly focus on improving supervision signal presented to the policy (Zhou et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2026). Yu et al. (2026) co-train the user to avoid overfitting. Our work identifies that issues may lie in all three parts, i.e., RL training dynamics, user simulation and environment, and we endeavor to address all at once with meta agent, EAU. Meta-Agents and Automated Optimization of Training Components. growing body of work uses one LLM to optimize another system or the system in which it operates (Hu et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Surina et al., 2025). EAU differs mainly in that the meta-agent acts within run: modifications are validated and hot-swapped into live training loop rather than applied between runs or before training begins. Co-evolution of Agent and its World. More recently, theres trend in improving the world, e.g., environment and user simulator, that an agent is interacting with. While most of them prepare the worlds before training (Huang et al., 2026; Tu et al., 2026), some begin to discover how the world can evolve along with the agent training (Yu et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026). Unlike prior methods that evolve the world through predefined update rules or workflows, EAU can flexibly determine what to modify, when to intervene, and how to adapt the training system online.

sections.title: 4 METHOD: ENVIRONMENT-AGENT-USER CO-EVOLUTION
sections.content: In this section, we introduce EAU (Environment-Agent-User Co-Evolution) for user-centric agentic RL. Recall that agentic RL with simulated users presents several challenges. First, sparse rewards and stochastic interactions can make learning difficult. Second, user simulators may provide unreliable rewards, deviate from instructions, or leak answers during conversations. 4.1 METHOD OVERVIEW The core idea of EAU is to couple policy learning with adaptation of the system that generates its training experience. The agent is updated through RL, while meta-agent uses training trajectories and optimization statistics to revise the user simulator, environment, and configurable training dynamics. These revisions change the interactions and learning signals encountered by subsequent policy updates, closing the feedback loop between policy behavior and training-system adaptation. We use co-evolution to denote this meta-agent-mediated, asymmetric co-adaptation. It does not require the environment and user simulator to be independently learned models: their adaptation is implemented through programmatic interventions. As illustrated in Figure 3, the meta-agent observes training feedback, selects interventions through editable interfaces, and accumulates experience for subsequent decisions. The following subsections describe the user-, environment-, and agent-side interventions, followed by their coordination within and across training runs. 4 Preprint: EAU, Meta-Agent for Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution

sections.title: 4.2 EVOLVING USER
sections.content: are LLM-simulated inherently users stochastic and may imperfectly follow its specification, for example by revealing information that should remain hidden or by improvising answers to questions unsupported by the task. To provide more controllable signal, we introduce symbolic user simulator, usym, which consists of set of explicit rules that deterministically map interaction states, obtained from parsed agent outputs, to user responses. Figure 4 illustrates an example of such rule. These rules provide precise control over what information is revealed and under which conditions. However, designing and updating them manually throughout training is intricate and labor-intensive. We therefore expose the symbolic rules as tunable knobs, allowing the meta-agent to revise them in response to the agents evolving behavior. Figure 4: Illustration of symbolic user simulator. The symbolic and LLM simulators offer complementary strengths: the former provides controllability and determinism, while the latter offers richer and more natural interactions. We combine them through an ϵ-symbolic strategy: uϵ := (cid:26)usym, with probability ϵ, uLLM, with probability 1 ϵ, ϵ [0, 1]. (2) The mixing coefficient ϵ thus controls the balance between structured, deterministic supervision and flexible LLM-based interaction, and can itself be adapted by the meta-agent during training. Beyond the symbolic rules and mixture coefficient ϵ, EAU can also evolve the LLM user by tuning controllable generation parameters, including temperature and persona-specific prompt instructions. Together, these mechanisms allow the user side of the training loop to adapt alongside the policy rather than remaining fixed throughout training. 4.3 EVOLVING ENVIRONMENT Environment-side adaptation in EAU modifies the training feedback and supported interaction conditions, rather than learning new world model. In our implementation, this primarily involves adding or revising intermediate reward signals in R, together with benchmarkspecific interaction constraints such as episode length. Recall that user-centric agentic tasks typically involve multi-turn interactions, where verifiable rewards are often sparse, such as task success. As result, the agent may struggle to explore effectively when it rarely reaches successful outcomes. When such behavior is observed, EAU can introduce intermediate reward rules that identify and reward states indicative of progress toward task completion. An illustrative example is shown in Figure 5. Figure 5: Illustration of environment evolution by introducing additional rewards. EAU can also revise existing manually designed rewards when they induce undesirable behaviors or divert the agent from the final objective. By dynamically adding and modifying intermediate rewards, EAU provides more informative learning signals while also accumulating experience about 5 Preprint: EAU, Meta-Agent for Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution which reward designs facilitate or hinder learning. This experience can in turn guide future environment evolution.

sections.title: 4.4 EVOLVING AGENT
sections.content: The agent naturally evolves through gradient updates during RL training. We keep the underlying training algorithm fixed and let the meta-agent continuously monitor the optimization process and intervene in its configurable training dynamics when necessary. Training Algorithm. We use and fix Proximal Policy Optimization (Schulman et al., 2017, PPO) as the RL algorithm. Recent work on LLM RL mainly use critic-free methods, such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), for low training cost and unbiased advantage estimation. However, current critic-free methods suffer from the sparse credit assignment, where intermediate rewards are accumulated to single trajectory-level reward (Qian et al., 2025b), or are not applicable to user-centric tasks where the same states are hard to replicate for group advantage estimation (Feng et al., 2026). We therefore use learned critic Vϕ, parameterized by ϕ, with Generalized Advantage Estimation ϕ = E[(Vϕ(q, y<t)R)2], where (GAE). The critic is optimized by minimizing the value error LVF is the cumulative reward. Both critic and policy are restricted to action tokens: the critic is evaluated only where the policy acts, and GAE is computed across actions rather than across all tokens, so the advantage of turn is not diluted by the observation text surrounding it (Hou et al., 2026). Formally, the advantage ˆAGAE is computed as: ˆAGAE = yt1 (cid:88) (γλ)lδt+l, l=0 (3) where δt = rt + γVϕ(st+1) Vϕ(st), and st refers to the t-th action token. Monitoring Training During training, the meta agent is allowed to tune the hyper-parameters such as entropy coefficient and KL coefficient, based on training logs, including metrics like estimated rollout entropy and log likelihood. It can also read the rollout trajectories and the interactions with the environment and the user. 4.5 INTRAAND INTER-RUN INTERVENTION notable design choice of EAU is to support flexible intervention at two timescales: both intra-run and inter-run. As illustrated in Figure 3, for intra-run intervention, updates can be hot-swapped into the training loop without restarting from scratch. For example, EAU can revise symbolic-user rules, add or modify environmental rewards, and adjust RL hyperparameters during training. It can also decide when restart (inter-run) is necessary, such as after an irreversible failure, or resume from an intermediate checkpoint. Inter-run intervention, in contrast, enables EAU to consolidate observations from completed runs and use them to revise the setup for subsequent training. Unlike previous paradigm that only allows inter-run modifications (Chen et al., 2026a; Xia et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025; Ferreira et al., 2026), by granting this flexibility, EAU can explore different operations on-the-fly, which is more efficient than inter-run interventions alone. Therefore, it can find out more effective operations based on the intraand inter-run experience. 4.6 INSTANTIATION OF META-AGENT We instantiate our meta agent with coding agents, such as Claude Code and Codex, following recent works on meta agent (Lee et al., 2026). The meta agent has access to local filesystem which includes the source code, training logs, etc. It reads the logs with fixed interval during training, and decides which part to modify for environment-user-agent evolution. list of knobs to tune is prepared at the beginning, but EAU can also modify the list if necessary. It is also asked to maintain experience pool as directory of documents in the filesystem. sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 5.1 EVALUATION PROTOCOL We evaluate EAU on three user-centric benchmarks. Experiments on UserGym and ColBench use two policy backbones, Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025) and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2025), while the τ 2-bench experiments use Qwen3-4B. We follow the benchmark evaluation protocol of Kong et al. (2026). Benchmarks. We consider ColBench (Zhou et al., 2025), UserGym (Qian et al., 2025b), and τ 2-bench (Barres et al., 2025). These benchmarks require agents to uncover hidden information through conversation and tool calls to fulfill users requests. Benchmark details are provided in Appendix B. Baselines. We compare against prompting methods (ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023)) and RL training methods (RAGEN (Wang et al., 2025b), Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025), UserRL (Qian et al., 2025b), and InfoPO (Kong et al., 2026)). We also include vanilla PPO. For UserGym and ColBench, baseline results other than PPO are taken from Kong et al. (2026). generic meta-agent baseline is additionally examined in our ablations. User simulator. The default training-time LLM simulator is CoSER (Wang et al., 2025a), finetuned Llama-3.1-8B model. This choice is motivated by its competitive user-simulation performance Preprint: EAU, Meta-Agent for Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution reported by Zhou et al. (2026). During training, EAU may replace the simulator when justified by the training logs. For evaluation, we use GPT-4o-mini, following Kong et al. (2026). Evaluation and model selection. Evaluation is performed after each completed training run. We report the final run and its final checkpoint for each experiment, without using final-test feedback for selection. Evaluation instances, trajectories, scores, and derived summaries are not used to propose or accept interventions, update the experience pool, or guide subsequent training runs. Training-side modifications do not alter the evaluation task set, user-simulator configuration, interaction limits, or scoring rules. 5.

The default episode limits are 16 turns on UserGym, 10 on ColBench, and 50 on τ 2-bench, with per-turn generation budget of 1024 tokens and per-episode rollout budgets of 8192, 8192, and 16384 tokens, respectively. Our analysis focuses on capabilities that support autonomous training intervention, rather than treating every editable component as an independently beneficial module. Ablation on symbolic user. Table 3 compares LLM, symbolic, and hybrid user simulators on ColBench. For Hybrid, we set the mixing coefficient to ϵ = 0.5. The hybrid simulator achieves slightly higher mean Pass and Succ. scores than the LLM-only simulator, whereas the symbolic-only variant performs worse. One possible explanation is that mixing more constrained symbolic responses with varied LLM responses preserves interaction diversity while providing more controlled feedback. Ablation on EAU design. Table 4 compares EAU with generic meta-agent constructed by removing the symbolic user and the skill for intra-run operations over the user, environment, and agent. This baseline receives only generic instruction to improve RL training. Compared with PPO, it produces mixed results, including decrease in UserGym performance on Qwen2.5-7BInstruct. EAU outperforms this baseline on both benchmarks and both policy backbones. Because the symbolic user and intervention skill are removed together, this comparison evaluates the combined design rather than their individual effects. Analysis: Alternative training algorithms and meta-agents. Table 5 shows that EAU improves aggregate performance when combined with either UserRL or InfoPO on τ 2-bench. The observed gains are therefore not restricted to the default PPO setup. Replacing the default meta-agent with Codex (GPT-5.6-Sol) also improves over InfoPO alone, although the gain is smaller than with the default meta-agent. These results demonstrate compatibility with multiple training and meta-agent configurations, with gains of different magnitudes across the tested configurations. Analysis: Intra-run exploration and experience reuse. We examine how intra-run intervention supports exploration of training modifications and reuse of the resulting experience. On ColBench, EAU proactively restarts its first three runs after detecting severe issues (Figures 1 and 6). It then explores multiple modifications in run 4 and carries these observations into run 5, the second completed run, which surpasses the strongest prior baseline. The generic inter-run meta-agent makes smaller gains over its run sequence. This progression illustrates how intra-run feedback can inform both immediate changes and subsequent training runs. Figure 7 further examines experience reuse on UserGym. Given the same experience from the first four runs, enabling intra-run intervention in run 5 yields larger improvement than inter-run adaptation alone. This supports the benefit of intra-run intervention in the illustrated setting. The curves show progression by run count, rather than an efficiency comparison under matched total compute. 9 Preprint: EAU, Meta-Agent for Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution Figure 6: Best-score frontiers on ColBench for EAU and the generic meta-agent. Each frontier tracks the best score observed so far and remains flat after unsuccessful or lower-scoring runs. Figure 7: Run-level progression on UserGym with Qwen3-4B. The two conditions share experience from the first four runs; in run 5, one uses inter-run adaptation only, while the other additionally permits intra-run intervention.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced EAU, meta-agent framework that jointly evolves the environment, agent, and user during training. We show that frontier coding agent can effectively manage and adapt these components based solely on training feedback, including trajectories and optimization logs. To provide finer control over user behavior, we introduce symbolic user simulator that the meta-agent can modify programmatically. We further enable intra-run interventions, allowing EAU to explore and exploit training modifications more flexibly. Across three user-centric benchmarks, EAU improves upon prior state-of-the-art performance by up to 36.7%. This highlights the value of adapting the training system itself. Future work may investigate post-training open-source models to perform such co-evolution autonomously.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: Our study concerns RL agents interacting with simulated users in benchmark environments; it does not recruit human participants or collect new human-participant data. EAU can modify training code, rewards, and user-simulator behavior, creating risks of implementation errors, misleading learning signals, and unintended task-information disclosure. The documented interface checks constrain admissible updates but do not guarantee behavioral correctness. Training-time adaptation is separated from fixed evaluation protocol, and final-test feedback is not used to guide interventions or select reported models. These controls address experimental integrity rather than establish deployment safety. Performance in simulated benchmarks should not be interpreted as evidence of safe or reliable behavior with real users.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: Section 4 describes the framework and meta-agent workflow. Section 5 specifies the benchmarks, model configurations, baselines, evaluation and model-selection protocol, and training and search limits. Appendix documents the intervention interfaces, benchmark-specific support, and recorded intervention outcomes. Additional benchmark and optimization details are provided in Appendices and C. We report standard deviations across repeated evaluations where available; these do not by themselves quantify variability across independent repetitions of the full training and adaptation process. Reproducing the reported configurations requires access to the external coding-agent and user-simulator models used in the experiments. 10 Preprint: EAU, Meta-Agent for Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: Generative AI is functional component of the proposed method and experimental pipeline. We use coding agents, including Claude Code and Codex, to inspect training logs and trajectories and propose or implement changes to the training system. LLMs also serve as policy models, user simulators, and evaluation components, as specified in Section 5. Beyond these experimental roles, generative AI tools assisted with manuscript revision, LaTeX preparation, and discussion of experimental interpretation. The authors retain responsibility for the research design, implementation, validation of reported results, and all final interpretations and claims. sections.title: B DETAILS ON EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Baselines. We compare EAU against both prompting-based and RL-based baselines. For prompting, we include ReAct (Yao et al., 2022), which interleaves reasoning with actions, and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), which improves agent behavior through verbal feedback and self-reflection. 16 Preprint: EAU, Meta-Agent for Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution Figure 8: Experience flow from UserGym, Qwen3-4B to ColBench, Qwen2.5-7B. For RL training, we consider RAGEN (Wang et al., 2025b), general multi-turn agent RL framework; Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025), which trains agents through reinforcement learning over multistep search trajectories; UserRL (Qian et al., 2025b), which targets interactive user-centric agents; and InfoPO (Kong et al., 2026), which introduces information-driven optimization for user-agent interaction. We additionally include vanilla PPO as standard RL baseline to isolate the gains from our co-evolution framework. For UserGym and ColBench, all baseline results except PPO are taken from Kong et al. (2026); PPO and EAU are evaluated under our implementation. Benchmarks. We evaluate our method on three representative user-centric benchmarks, i.e., ColBench (Zhou et al., 2025), UserGym (Qian et al., 2025b), and τ 2-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Barres et al., 2025). ColBench evaluates collaborative artifact creation, where the agent works with an LLM-simulated collaborator that has privileged access to hidden reference artifact. We evaluate EAU on the Backend Programming subset, where the agent implements Python function from an incomplete specification, and is evaluated with hidden unit tests. UserGym is suite of eight Gymnasium environments unified under single tool interface, spanning preference elicitation, intent clarification, entity guessing, lateral-thinking puzzles, rule induction, policy-constrained tool use, persuasion, and search. Each episode pairs rule-based task with an LLM-simulated user who holds the ground-truth intent and reveals it only when queried. Because the initial request is systematically underspecified, the agent must repeatedly trade off asking the user against committing to an action. We report the environment reward averaged within and across gyms. Specifically, we exclude the SearchGym for evaluation due to the cost of APIs. It requires the agent to conduct online search using charged api. Notably, this does not affect the RL training, since its an OOD gym solely for evaluation. τ 2-bench casts customer service as dual-control problem in which both the agent and the simulated user can act on shared world state. Unlike prior benchmarks where the user is passive information source, the user here has its own tools, so the agent must verbally guide the user through actions it cannot perform itself while complying with domain policy. We evaluate on the retail, airline, and telecom domains, and score task as solved only when the resulting environment state matches the annotated target and all required information has been conveyed to the user.
